C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

  /-
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    r : F.World
    F_refl : Reflexive F.Rel
    F_eucl : Euclidean F.Rel
    ⊢ Universal (F.PointGenerated r).Rel
  -/

  /-
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    r : F.World
    F_refl : Reflexive F.Rel
    F_eucl : Euclidean F.Rel
    F_symm : Symmetric F.Rel
    ⊢ Universal (F.PointGenerated r).Rel
  -/
  rintro ⟨x, (rfl | hx)⟩ ⟨y, (rfl | hy)⟩;
    /-
      case mk.inl.mk.inl
      F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
      F_refl : Reflexive F.Rel
      F_eucl : Euclidean F.Rel
      F_symm : Symmetric F.Rel
      y : F.World
      ⊢ (F.PointGenerated y).Rel ⟨y, ⋯⟩ ⟨y, ⋯⟩
    -/
  . apply F_refl;
    /-
      🎉 no goals
    -/
    /-
      case mk.inl.mk.inr
      F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
      F_refl : Reflexive F.Rel
      F_eucl : Euclidean F.Rel
      F_symm : Symmetric F.Rel
      x y : F.World
      hy : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame.Rel' x y
      ⊢ (F.PointGenerated x).Rel ⟨x, ⋯⟩ ⟨y, ⋯⟩
    -/
  . exact hy;
    /-
      🎉 no goals
    -/
    /-
      case mk.inr.mk.inl
      F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
      F_refl : Reflexive F.Rel
      F_eucl : Euclidean F.Rel
      F_symm : Symmetric F.Rel
      x y : F.World
      hx : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame.Rel' y x
      ⊢ (F.PointGenerated y).Rel ⟨x, ⋯⟩ ⟨y, ⋯⟩
    -/
  . exact F_symm hx;
    /-

      case mk.inr.mk.inr

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

  ∀ b, ∃ a, f a = b

annotation:
lemma iff_formula_valid_on_frame_surjective_morphism (f : F₁ →ₚ F₂) (f_surjective : Function.Surjective f) : F₁ ⊧ φ → F₂ ⊧ φ := by
  /-
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    ⊢ LO.Semantics.Realize F₁ φ → LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ
  -/
  contrapose;
  /-
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    ⊢ Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ) → Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₁ φ)
  -/
  intro h;
  /-
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    h : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ)
    ⊢ Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₁ φ)
  -/
  obtain ⟨V₂, w₂, h⟩ := by simpa [ValidOnFrame, ValidOnModel] using h;
  /-
    case intro.intro
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    h✝ : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ)
    V₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Valuation F₂
    w₂ : F₂.World
    h : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize w₂ φ)
    ⊢ Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₁ φ)
  -/
  simp [ValidOnFrame, ValidOnModel];

  /-
    case intro.intro
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    h✝ : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ)
    V₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Valuation F₂
    w₂ : F₂.World
    h : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize w₂ φ)
    ⊢ Exists fun x => Exists fun x_1 => Not (LO.Semantics.Realize x_1 φ)
  -/
  obtain ⟨w₁, e⟩ := f_surjective w₂; subst e;
  /-
    case intro.intro.intro
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    h✝ : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ)
    V₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Valuation F₂
    w₁ : F₁.World
    h : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize (f.toFun w₁) φ)
    ⊢ Exists fun x => Exists fun x_1 => Not (LO.Semantics.Realize x_1 φ)
  -/
  let V₁ := λ w a => V₂ (f w) a;
  /-
    case intro.intro.intro
    F₁ F₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    f : F₁.PseudoEpimorphism F₂
    f_surjective : Function.Surjective f.toFun
    h✝ : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize F₂ φ)
    V₂ : LO.Modal.Kripke.Valuation F₂
    w₁ : F₁.World
    h : Not (LO.Semantics.Realize (f.toFun w₁) φ)
    V₁ : F₁.World → Nat → Prop := fun w a => V₂ (f.toFun w) a
    ⊢ Exists fun x => Exists fun x_1 => Not (LO.Semantics.Realize x_1 φ)
  -/
  use V₁, w₁;

  exact Model.PseudoEpimorphism.modal_equivalence (M₁ := ⟨F₁, V₁⟩) (M₂ := ⟨F₂, V₂⟩) {
    toFun := f,
    forth := f.forth,
    back := f.back,
    atomic := by aesop;
  } w₁ |>.not.mpr h;

for some `a : α`. -/
def Surjective (f : α → β) : Prop :=
  ∀ b, ∃ a, f a = b

/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

def rec' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
  (hfalsum : C ⊥)
  (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
  (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ➝ ψ))
  (hbox    : ∀ (φ : Formula α), C φ → C (□φ))
  : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥      => hfalsum
  | atom a => hatom a
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hatom himp hbox φ) (rec' hfalsum hatom himp hbox ψ)
  | □φ     => hbox φ (rec' hfalsum hatom himp hbox φ)

import Foundation.Modal.Kripke.Closure


namespace LO.Modal

namespace Kripke

open Formula.Kripke


section Bisimulation

structure Model.Bisimulation (M₁ M₂ : Kripke.Model) where
  toRel : Rel M₁.World M₂.World
  atomic {x₁ : M₁.World} {x₂ : M₂.World} {a : ℕ} : toRel x₁ x₂ → ((M₁ x₁ a) ↔ (M₂ x₂ a))
  forth {x₁ y₁ : M₁.World} {x₂ : M₂.World} : toRel x₁ x₂ → x₁ ≺ y₁ → ∃ y₂ : M₂.World, toRel y₁ y₂ ∧ x₂ ≺ y₂
  back {x₁ : M₁.World} {x₂ y₂ : M₂.World} : toRel x₁ x₂ → x₂ ≺ y₂ → ∃ y₁ : M₁.World, toRel y₁ y₂ ∧ x₁ ≺ y₁

infix:80 " ⇄ " => Model.Bisimulation

instance : CoeFun (Model.Bisimulation M₁ M₂) (λ _ => M₁.World → M₂.World → Prop) := ⟨λ bi => bi.toRel⟩

end Bisimulation


section ModalEquivalent

def ModalEquivalent {M₁ M₂ : Model} (w₁ : M₁.World) (w₂ : M₂.World) : Prop := ∀ {φ}, w₁ ⊧ φ ↔ w₂ ⊧ φ

import Foundation.Modal.Kripke.Closure


namespace LO.Modal

namespace Kripke

open Formula.Kripke


section Bisimulation

structure Model.Bisimulation (M₁ M₂ : Kripke.Model) where
  toRel : Rel M₁.World M₂.World
  atomic {x₁ : M₁.World} {x₂ : M₂.World} {a : ℕ} : toRel x₁ x₂ → ((M₁ x₁ a) ↔ (M₂ x₂ a))
  forth {x₁ y₁ : M₁.World} {x₂ : M₂.World} : toRel x₁ x₂ → x₁ ≺ y₁ → ∃ y₂ : M₂.World, toRel y₁ y₂ ∧ x₂ ≺ y₂
  back {x₁ : M₁.World} {x₂ y₂ : M₂.World} : toRel x₁ x₂ → x₂ ≺ y₂ → ∃ y₁ : M₁.World, toRel y₁ y₂ ∧ x₁ ≺ y₁

infix:80 " ⇄ " => Model.Bisimulation

instance : CoeFun (Model.Bisimulation M₁ M₂) (λ _ => M₁.World → M₂.World → Prop) := ⟨λ bi => bi.toRel⟩

end Bisimulation


section ModalEquivalent

def ModalEquivalent {M₁ M₂ : Model} (w₁ : M₁.World) (w₂ : M₂.World) : Prop := ∀ {φ}, w₁ ⊧ φ ↔ w₂ ⊧ φ
infix:50 " ↭ " => ModalEquivalent
annotation: infix:50 " ↭ " => ModalEquivalent
